Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Reverend Amara Nwosu remembered the dry dust of the displacement camp, the year the fighting reached her village. She had been herded onto rattling transport buses by men whose hands never left the rifles slung across their chests. When a passenger shifted too quickly or a crate was dropped, the guards would spin, weapons raised, voices cracking with violence. In those cramped carriages, she was not treated as a woman or a mother, but as cargo stacked beside strangers. The air grew thick with sweat and fear, and soon the boundary between herself and the space around her dissolved. What frightened her most was how easily the guards had stripped her of her dignity, reducing her to an object to be moved at their whim, with no one anywhere to question their cruelty. Decades later, Amara’s past lived in the present through the sight of a passing vehicle or the glint of a tool on a contractor’s belt. Whenever she rode the city bus to visit her sister, the moment the driver braked sharply or a stranger brushed past her seat, her body snapped into immediate defense. She was certain that any sudden gesture could spark the same sudden violence, so she found herself constantly scanning the faces in front of her and glancing over her shoulder to see if the threat was still pursuing her. Those fleeting moments of tension would pull the past straight into her awareness; the bus’s engine would rumble into the exact cadence of the convoy’s diesel, and she would hear the guards’ shouts echoing in her mind, unbidden and raw. When the ride made her feel detached from her own body, she interpreted the unreality as proof that she was still being treated as property, deepening her conviction that what happened to her was deeply unfair. The memories did not arrive as coherent stories she could control. They forced their way into her mind during quiet moments in the parsonage, their intensity making her doubt her own sanity. She had come to believe that if she let herself sit with the recollection, the weight would crush her entirely, so she refused to speak of it with her husband, her congregation, or any counselor. This belief that she could not handle the thoughts meant they were left to fester, so when her guard dropped, the intrusive memories and auditory flashes forced their way in unbidden. Her conviction that she was powerless against arbitrary cruelty meant she watched other people closely for signs that they might harm her, which in turn flooded her with the sensory echoes of the displacement. Because she felt as though she were still being treated as an object rather than a person, even the sight of a uniform or the sound of a crowded stoppage could instantly reignite her fear, pulling her back into the cycle of hyperarousal. By refusing to talk about what she had endured, Amara denied herself the chance to process the trauma, leaving the uncontrolled memories to multiply in the silence. She avoided medical appointments altogether, fearing that a doctor’s office might trigger the same suffocating claustrophobia she felt on public transport. When the bus rattled past her window or a maintenance worker’s tool caught the light, the sudden sensory hit drove her to pull her coat tighter and cancel her next visit. This pattern of avoidance only amplified her sensitivity to environmental cues; the mere thought of boarding a bus or encountering someone with a metallic object on their belt would spike her anxiety, making her body brace for impact before a single threat actually appeared. Her habit of concealing herself and sidestepping care did not shield her from the past. While preparing communion at the altar, a deacon’s quick movement to hand her a chalice made her drop the linen, instantly pulling her back to the bus carriages. The loop tightened with each passing week, each avoided appointment, each guarded glance, until her daily routine became a narrow circuit of dread. The exhaustion of maintaining this constant guard eroded her ability to lead her congregation as she once had, and her husband noticed how she flinched at loud noises and refused to leave the neighborhood without her coat pulled high. The constant state of watchfulness reinforced her dehumanization, as if her own survival required her to suppress her humanity. What she most hoped for was simply to rest without dread, yet she feared that reaching out would force her to relive the injustice that had stolen her peace long ago.
